description: ODC (EDIT and REFACTORING coverage): touch the platform events that THIS job did not create. The base is job:external-site-and-events, that is, the ISystemEvent (OnApplicationReady), the two IEvent (Extended Events) and the screen action that handles them already exist when the first op runs; there is no create from scratch of these types here, on purpose, because creating and editing in the same job proves no maintenance at all. Outside the job that declared them there are no aliases: each inherited object is cited as 'ISystemEvent:OnApplicationReady', 'IEvent:onclick', 'IClientVariable:WfCovLastOpenedAt', and the children by path ('ISystemEvent:OnApplicationReady/#IAssignNode[1]/#IAssignment[1]'). Four things are proven, and two of them are measured REFUSALS. (1) THE SYSTEM EVENT HANDLER is a normal logic flow and is edited as such: this job rewrites the Value of the inherited IAssignment, adds a SECOND IAssignment to the SAME inherited IAssignNode and fixes the Label that was left lying - none of this required touching the unique place <espace>.#OnApplicationReady, which remains the same object with the same key. (2) THE NAME OF THE EXTENDED EVENT IS NOT RENAMED, BUT IT CHANGES: 'rename' on an IEvent is refused by the PLATFORM, before the kernel even gets to its own 'Name is read-only' - the exact message, measured in this build, is 'op #N (rename <name>): InvalidOperationException: Cannot find handler for object On Click of type Event.', thrown from ServiceStudio.Model.NameClashHandler.GetNamesToNameClashAgainstChildObj, because the Events collection has no name-clash handler (ExtendedEvent.Name is a sealed getter that returns the EventName). The ONLY way to change its name is to write 'Event': this job sets onclick to ondoubleclick and the following get shows DisplayName and ReadableIdentifier following on their own. (3) THE SAME REFUSAL CATCHES THE SYSTEM EVENT, for the same reason and from the same factory: 'op #N (rename WfEvtOnStart): InvalidOperationException: Cannot find handler for object OnApplicationReady of type On Application Ready.' - OnApplicationReady is not a named sibling in a collection, it is a unique place of the IESpace, so there is nothing to compare the name against. Neither refusal can live in a green job (an op that raises aborts the run); they are kept here by their exact text, and the contrast is in the ops: the inherited IExternalSite, a flow neighbor of both, is renamed without a complaint and the Destination of the button stays linked by key. (4) WHAT IS REFACTORED AROUND THE EVENT FOLLOWS IT: renaming the inherited IClientVariable rewrites the TWO expressions that read it - the one of the IAssignment inside the system event and the one of the screen -; renaming the inherited screen action does not move a byte in the two IEvent, because Handler is a link by KEY and not by name; and a 'replace' of the old action by the new one repointed the remaining handler without the IEvent changing key, which left the old one with zero consumers and the delete passed without force. Note on the data contract of this run, measured and not assumed: the contract closed with THREE assertions and no difference, and which ones they are contradicts the naive reading of the stable-identity list. 'ISystemEvent' is NOT in that list, and even so the Description this job writes to it IS watched: the list is compared against the short type name AND against ALL the interfaces the real object implements, and the real object behind OnApplicationReady is a ServiceStudio.Model.SystemClientActions.OnApplicationReady, which implements IClientAction - that one is in the list. The IEvent, on the other hand, gets in by no path (neither ExtendedEvent nor its interfaces are there), nor does the IClientVariable: this job's writes to 'Event' and to 'Handler' are not checked on their own, and that is why each one carries here its read-back get, by hand. The third lesson is in what is MISSING: the job writes Description on TWO screen actions and only one appears in the contract, because the other was deleted by the job itself in op (14d) - an assertion on an object the job deleted on purpose is not a lost proof, it is a fulfilled proof, and the contract drops it instead of failing the run.

ops.name: WfCovNormalizeSearch
ops._why: (0) the starting point is INHERITED: the screen action that handles the two Extended Events already exists before the first op of this job. It came from job:external-site-and-events, not from a create here

(1) BEFORE, the inherited system event: the key is <espace>.#OnApplicationReady (unique place of the IESpace, not a collection), Nodes=3 and IsValid=True - unlike the creation, where the flow came empty and invalid. Description is null: the edit job is the one that will write it
(2) BEFORE, the handler tree: Start -> RememberOpenedAt (an IAssignment) -> End. This is the snapshot the dump (22) is compared with

(3) BEFORE, the inherited payload: Variable 'Client.WfCovLastOpenedAt' and Value 'FormatDateTime(CurrDateTime(), "yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm")'. The path is by position because an IAssignNode has no Name - it has a Label, and the Label does not serve as a segment

(4) BEFORE, the Extended Event of the container: Event=onclick, Handler pointing at the inherited screen action, and NO Name property in the list - the 'name' the get shows comes from TypeResolver, which reads the derived DisplayName. This absence is what explains the rename refusal described in the description
(5) BEFORE, the second Extended Event, inside the IInput: Handler with the SAME key as the first - one handler, two events

(6) BEFORE: count=real=2, byType IEvent:2. The two consumers of the inherited screen action are the two Extended Events, and the paths show where they live (one in the IContainer, the other inside the IInput)

(7a) CHANGE 1 - the system event handler. Rewrite the Value of an IAssignment that another job wrote: the precision now has seconds. It is the case only an edit job shows - the text being replaced is not an empty field, it is the expression the creation job left there

ops.name: WfEvtOpenCount
ops._why: (7b) the second half of change 1 needs somewhere to write. It is the only top-level element this job creates, and it carries the Wf prefix

ops.value: Quantas vezes a app arrancou. Acrescentado por platform-events-lifecycle.json ao handler que ja existia.

ops._why: (7c) CHANGE 1, continued: a SECOND IAssignment inside the INHERITED IAssignNode. The node was not recreated - its key is the same as in get (2) - it just started doing one more thing
(7d) the inherited Label started lying as soon as the node gained the second assignment. Fixing it is maintenance work: the Label is author text, it follows nothing on its own

ops.value: Arranque da app: marca a hora e conta a abertura. Description escrita por platform-events-lifecycle.json, depois de o fluxo existir.
ops._why: (7e) the system event itself accepts Description, and the get (7f) reads it back. This is also the write that teaches how far the data contract of this run reaches: 'ISystemEvent' is not in the stable-identity list, but the assertion appears anyway in the final contract, because the real object is a SystemClientActions.OnApplicationReady and the watch tests ALL the implemented interfaces - and one of them is IClientAction. The system event is watched for what it IS, not for the name the job calls it by
(7f) AFTER, compare with get (1): the Description CHANGED; the key, Nodes=3 and IsValid=True STAYED. Nodes stays 3 because change 1 added an ASSIGNMENT, not a node
(7g) AFTER, the inherited node: Assignments went from 1 to 2 and the Label is the new one, with the SAME Key as get (2) - it was edited, not replaced

(8a) BEFORE change 2: count=real=2, and the two consumers are ITextBasedExpression - one inside the system event (the Variable of the IAssignment), the other on the screen (the expression that shows the time). A client variable read on both sides of the app

ops.name: WfEvtLastOpenedAt
ops._why: (8b) CHANGE 2 - rename an INHERITED variable that the system event handler writes. It returns consumers=2 and expressionsRewritten=2: here the counter is honest because the consumers THEMSELVES are the expressions; in the rename of an aggregate node the same counter says something else (see refactor-inherited.json)

(8c) READ BACK, and it is the proof: the Variable of the inherited IAssignment already says 'Client.WfEvtLastOpenedAt' without a hand correction, and the Value is the one from change 1 (with seconds). In the O11 lane this same expression would have stayed with the old name
(8d) the same two consumers, with the same keys and the text already rewritten on both sides: the rename touched the text, not the link

(9a) CHANGE 3 - touch the inherited IEvent. 'Event' is the CLOSED list of 11 names of the product; writing there is the only way to change the name of this object, because the rename is refused by the platform (exact message in the description). From here on the same object no longer answers to 'IEvent:onclick'

(9b) AFTER: the SAME Key as get (4), Handler intact, and DisplayName/ReadableIdentifier went on their own to 'ondoubleclick'. The name of the Extended Event is DERIVED from the event - it is renamed from inside, never through the rename verb

ops.name: WfEvtClearSearch
ops._why: (10a) the NEW handler for change 4. It is born on the INHERITED screen and without outputs, which is what the real Handler descriptor requires (DestinationPropertyDescriptor<ExtendedEvent, IExecutableWebDestinationWithNoOutputs>)

ops.value: Limpa a pesquisa. Passa a ser o handler mantido dos Extended Events desta tela.

ops._why: (10b) CHANGE 4 - swap the HANDLER of an inherited Extended Event. It is a property like any other: the event keeps the same key and now points to another action. The usages that follows shows the bookkeeping changing on both sides
(10c) AFTER, compare with get (5): the Handler CHANGED; Key, Event and the parent STAYED. It was the target that changed, not the consumer
(10d) the inherited action dropped from 2 consumers to 1 - only the Extended Event of the container (now ondoubleclick) still holds it

ops.value: Tela de cobertura dos eventos. Description escrita por platform-events-lifecycle.json sobre a tela herdada.
ops._why: (11) unlike the IEvent, which does not enter the contract by any path, IMobileScreen is in the stable-identity list by its own name: this write enters the end-of-run contract on its own and is checked there, without the job needing to ask

ops.value: Handler herdado da normalizacao da pesquisa. Vai ser renomeado e depois substituido neste mesmo job.
ops._why: the same for IScreenAction. Note that the Description is written BEFORE the rename and the delete: the contract stores the assertion by KEY, and the job's own deliberate deletion does not turn it into a lost proof

ops.name: WfEvtNormalizeSearch
ops._why: (12a) CHANGE 5 - rename the INHERITED action that an Extended Event still handles. It returns consumers=1 and expressionsRewritten=0, and the zero is honest: no expression reads the output of a screen action; what holds it is the Handler property of an IEvent
(12b) READ BACK: the Handler of the Extended Event has exactly the SAME key as before the rename. The link is by key; the name is only text the platform shows
(12c) the other side: new Name, same Key, Referrers=1, and the Description written in op (11) intact - renaming does not touch it
(13a) THE CONTRAST the description promises: the inherited external site lives in the SAME flow as the events and is the destination of the button. Referrers=1

ops.name: WfEvtDocsSite
ops._why: (13b) and THIS one is renamed without a complaint. It is the proof by comparison that the refusal on the two event types is not from the rename verb nor from the kernel: it is from the platform, which only has a name-clash handler for what is a named sibling in a collection
(13c) READ BACK: the IBuiltinEvent of the button keeps the same Destination, by key. Two event families on the same screen - IBuiltinEvent navigates, IEvent calls logic - and both link by key

(14a) CHANGE 6 - REPOINT the remaining consumer. The Studio's own ReplaceReferences reaches the Handler property of an ExtendedEvent (the class has the override for that); the event keeps the key and only changes target
(14b) the old one must end up with zero consumers
(14c) and the new handler now handles the TWO Extended Events - one by set (10b), the other by replace (14a). Same result, two different paths

(14d) after the replace there are no consumers, so the delete passes WITHOUT force and brokenConsumers=0. The inherited screen is left with a single handler, the kept one. This is where the data contract of this run loses one of the four possible assertions: the Description written in op (11) belonged to this action, and the contract drops by KEY what the job itself deleted, instead of failing the run with its own deletion

ops.name: WfCovNormalizeSearch
ops._why: (14e) empty list: the inherited name from op (0) disappeared from the module, and the model is still valid
(15a) close the circuit of change 1 inside the INHERITED container: without a reader, the counter written at startup proved nothing. The parent is the container the other job created
(16) the final state of the first inherited assignment: Variable with the new name of the variable, Value with the seconds. Two independent changes on the same line that another job wrote
(17) The final tree of the system event handler, set next to dump (2): the SAME three nodes, the corrected Label and TWO assignments where there was one. The flow was not rebuilt - it was edited

(18) The final tree of the inherited container: the IEvent now appears as ondoubleclick next to the content, the new counter expression entered at the end, and the second event is still deeper, inside the IInput
(19) WHAT REMAINED: the inherited screen with the new Description, ScreenActions=1 (it was 1: one came in and the other went out) and the SAME key. An edit job does not rebuild the screen underneath
